title: Not Quite Right
bodyHtml:
A chatbot is a computer program that is designed to have conversations with people. NacloCorp has recently developed a chatbot, and it is your job to test it out.

First, you ask NacloChat to decode five sentences written in a cipher, where each letter has been replaced by a different letter. The table below shows what you found, but some cells in the table are blank.

Cipher textCorrect answerNacloChat’s answer
IPVFDDN ZSJ DPQJ SFT BLQJa.finally the time has come
ZSJN BSFVZJG ZSJ LIIPBPFD ULDPBNb.they changed the official policy
SJ TZYIIJG ZSJ ULTZJW PVTPGJ F ZYEFc.he stuffed the poster inside a tube
ZSJN TFPDJG FXFN PV F ELLZd.e.
XJ QYTZ EJ APVG ZL JFBS LZZJWf.g.

F1. Fill in the blanks a. to g.

Hints:

  • The same cipher has been used in all five sentences. For example, if Q stands for m in the first sentence, it will stand for m in all other sentences too.
  • In each of the five sentences, NacloChat got exactly one letter wrong.

Next, you ask NacloChat to form acronyms from the names of several organizations. An acronym is created by combining the first letters from all the words in a sequence of words. The table below shows what you find.

OrganizationCorrect answerNacloChat’s answer
Waiting Room Enthusiasts NetworkWRENWHEN
Architects Building Office Units Near DesertsABOUNDAROUND
Seriously Creative Hat Manufacturers Organizational LeagueSCHMOLSCHOOL
Society Incentivizing Lateness — Earlybirds Not Allowed!SILENASILENT
People Improving Tomorrow’s YesterdayPITYCITY
Annoyingly Friendly Thimblemakers — Northern RegionAFTNRh.
Vancouver Eggplant Relocation BureauVERBi.
Pseudoscientists Embracing Obviously Counterfeited EvidencePEOCEj.
Filmmakers Reimagining Old MemoirsFROMk.
Western Indiana Typewriter SocietyWITSl.

F2. Fill in the cells h. to l. that are missing from the table.

Hints:

  • There is one case where NacloChat gets the right answer. In all other cases, it gets exactly one letter wrong.
  • The “Organization” column is provided for fun, but it is not necessary for solving the problem.

Finally, you ask NacloChat to count how many words there are in some lists of words. For example, given the list “elephant jacket spaghetti mattress,” NacloChat should answer 4. You observe that it sometimes gets the answer wrong.

F3. Below are some questions about three of the cases that NacloChat answered incorrectly. Select the correct letter (A or B) for each one. Note: To save some space, we are not providing the lists that were given to NacloChat — we are just saying how long each list was.

In the past few years, many chatbots — powered by a type of technology called large language models (LLMs) — have been developed that can perform impressively well on a wide range of tasks. For example, they can summarize text and write computer code. However, despite their impressive performance, there are certain types of situations where chatbots often have trouble. This problem illustrates one type of issue that many chatbots display.

questions.partPrompt: For each case, select the letter (A or B) of the number NacloChat produced.
questions.promptHtml: 1. When the length of the list was 91, what number did NacloChat produce?
2. When the length of the list was 59, what number did NacloChat produce?
3. When the length of the list was 74, what number did NacloChat produce?

hints.text: Start with the three rows where NacloChat's answer is given. Even though the chatbot made one mistake in each of those rows, almost every letter it produced is right, so you can use them to build a letter-by-letter key for the cipher (Z = t, S = h, J = e, and so on).

In every part, NacloChat's mistake makes the answer into something more ordinary or expected: an unusual word becomes a common word, a random-looking string of letters becomes a real English word, and an awkward number becomes a rounder number. Once you have decoded a sentence correctly, ask yourself which single letter a chatbot would 'fix' to get a more familiar sentence — and go the other way for the rows where you are given the chatbot's answer.

Worked step on ungraded data: in row 3 the cipher text ends with F ZYEF, and NacloChat says 'a tube'. Using the key, F = a, Z = t, Y = u, E = b, so ZYEF spells t-u-b-a. The chatbot changed the odd-sounding 'tuba' into the far more common 'tube' — exactly one letter off, in the direction of the more expected word.

explanationHtml:
What kind of puzzle is this?

There is one idea behind all three parts: NacloChat does not really carry out the task you asked for. Instead it produces the answer that looks most normal — the most familiar sentence, the most familiar word, the roundest number. Each time, its answer is only slightly off from the truth, and always slightly off in the direction of 'more ordinary'.

Part F1: cracking the cipher

A substitution cipher replaces every letter of the alphabet with some other letter, consistently. Because NacloChat gets only one letter wrong per sentence, its (mostly correct) answers are almost a free answer key.

Line up the first row:

IPVFDDNZSJDPQJSFTBLQJ
finallythe?imehascome

From IPVFDDN = finally we get I=f, P=i, V=n, F=a, D=l, N=y. From ZSJ = the: Z=t, S=h, J=e. From SFT = has: T=s. From BLQJ = come: B=c, L=o, Q=m.

Now check the third word, DPQJ. Using the key: D=l, P=i, Q=m, J=e → lime. NacloChat said time. That is the one letter it got wrong — and notice why: 'finally the time has come' is a phrase you have heard a thousand times, while 'finally the lime has come' is not. So a. finally the lime has come.

Row 2 works the same way. BSFVZJG = c-h-a-n-t-e-d (this also tells us G=d), so the true sentence is b. they chanted the official policy; the chatbot slid 'chanted' into the more expected 'changed'. Row 3 gives ZYEF = t-u-b-a (so Y=u, and from ULTZJW = poster we also get U=p, W=r), so c. he stuffed the poster inside a tuba.

Our key so far: A=k, B=c, D=l, E=b, F=a, G=d, I=f, J=e, L=o, N=y, P=i, Q=m, S=h, T=s, U=p, V=n, W=r, X=w, Y=u, Z=t.

Rows 4 and 5 have both cells blank, so decode them yourself and then predict the chatbot's slip:

  • ZSJN TFPDJG FXFN PV F ELLZ → they sailed away in a boot (ELLZ = b-o-o-t; FXFN = a-w-a-y gives X=w). That is odd, and the ordinary version is 'boat', so d. they sailed away in a boot and e. they sailed away in a boat.
  • XJ QYTZ EJ APVG ZL JFBS LZZJW → we must be kind to each otter (APVG = k-i-n-d gives A=k; LZZJW = o-t-t-e-r). The familiar saying is 'each other', so f. we must be kind to each otter and g. we must be kind to each other.

Part F2: acronyms

An acronym takes the first letter of each word. Look at what the chatbot does with the given examples: WREN → WHEN, ABOUND → AROUND, SCHMOL → SCHOOL, SILENA → SILENT, PITY → CITY. In every case it changes exactly one letter and lands on a very common English word of the same length.

So do the same for the blanks:

  • AFTNR → AFTER (N→E)
  • VERB → VERY (B→Y)
  • PEOCE → PEACE (O→A)
  • FROM → FROM — this one is already an extremely common word, so nothing gets 'fixed'. This is the promised case where NacloChat is right.
  • WITS → WITH (S→H)

Note that VERB and WITS are real words too, but not nearly as frequent as very and with; the chatbot drifts toward the highest-frequency neighbour.

Part F3: counting

Same principle, applied to numbers: the chatbot's answer is one off from the truth, in the direction of a 'rounder', more expected number (a multiple of 10, or at least of 5).

  • 91 → the neighbours are 90 and 92; 90 is round, so the answer is A. 90.
  • 59 → neighbours 58 and 60; 60 is round, so B. 60.
  • 74 → neighbours 73 and 75; 75 is the rounder one, so B. 75.

Why real chatbots behave this way

Large language models are trained to predict what text is likely to come next, based on huge amounts of writing. That makes them excellent at producing fluent, typical language — but when the correct answer is atypical (a rare phrase like 'each otter', a nonsense acronym like PEOCE, an unround count like 59), the pull toward the typical can override the actual task. Linguists call this kind of pressure a bias toward high-frequency forms, and this problem is built entirely out of it.
